title: You Really Don’t Know
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart tells the story of running into a former student, Scarlett, at a grocery store years after she was on his roster -- a student he'd long assumed he'd failed to reach, since she'd dropped out of high school. Scarlett tells him, unprompted and beaming, that the pop-up debates from his class helped her land a public-speaking role as a union steward at her job. The encounter becomes the article's thesis: teachers routinely underestimate their own impact because the evidence for it rarely shows up in the places they're trained to look -- tests, grades, diplomas. He generalizes from the anecdote to a broader claim about the hidden, long-tail nature of teaching's impact, urging worn-down teachers heading into spring to trust that the work is landing in ways they will mostly never see or be thanked for.
points: The anecdote's structural point: Stuart had been 'positive' for years that he'd failed Scarlett, and the disconfirming evidence only surfaced by chance, years later, in a grocery store -- illustrating how invisible real impact can be to the teacher who caused it.
His explicit thesis: 'you and I just don't know the extent of our impact,' and the tools schools use to measure success (tests, grades, diplomas) systematically miss this kind of long-tail effect.

He connects the specific classroom practice (pop-up debates) directly to Scarlett's later real-world outcome (a public-speaking job as a union steward), giving the abstract claim about impact a concrete causal thread.
He frames the piece as timed encouragement for a specific moment -- 'spring is coming, colleague' -- aimed at teachers running low on motivation before the anecdote's payoff arrives.
quotes: For years, I had been positive that I had failed with Scarlett — positive that, despite my efforts, I hadn't helped her grow as a thinker, speaker, reader, writer, or person.
You know, Mr. Stuart, your class helped me with public speaking. I used to hate it so much, but those pop-up debates showed me that I could do it.
But Scarlett didn't think that. Scarlett had evidence, years later, that the simple work we did in my class contributed at least a percentage point to the improvement of her long-term flourishing.
Tests didn't show it. Grades didn't show it. Her diploma didn't show it. But, nonetheless, there it was that day in the store, standing right in front of me with a big smile.
Here's the point: You and I just don't know the extent of our impact. Doing the right work with the attitude of a craftsperson is too wrought with potential.
For every thank you that you get from a student for the work you've done this year, there are untold dozens that you won't.
